lead: Both readings are about faith that holds. James says that trials are a chance for joy, because tested faith grows into endurance, and he tells the one who lacks wisdom to ask God, who gives generously, without doubting. In Mark, Jesus teaches his disciples, beside a fruitless fig tree, to have faith in God, to pray with confidence, and to forgive before they pray. Today the Church also keeps the memorial of the martyrs Sts Kuriakose and Julitta, mother and child, whose own readings (Daniel 3, Acts 6, Hebrews 11 and Matthew 10) show faith that stood in the fire; the readings of the day are the two exegeted here.

set: These are the opening lines of the Letter of James, addressed to the “twelve tribes in the Dispersion” (1:1): Jewish Christians living outside the land. They were under pressure, and James writes to strengthen them. The letter is traditionally ascribed to James, “the brother of the Lord”, though some scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name.
James does not begin with advice about avoiding trials. He begins with joy, a surprising joy that does not deny pain but sees what the trial can do.
str: vv. 2–4: trials, joy, testing of faith, endurance, maturity.
v. 5: the lack of wisdom: ask God, who gives generously.
vv. 6–8: ask in faith; the doubter is double-minded and unstable.
kw: The same word can mean a temptation to sin and a testing of faith; the context decides. Here it is the testing that the believer meets from outside, like gold tried in fire, and James has no fear of it.
Not passive waiting but staying power: remaining under the load and keeping faith. It is the quality that Jesus asks of disciples in the Gospels (Luke 21:19).
Literally “two-souled”: a person divided between God and something else. James uses it again in 4:8. It names the same split that causes quarrels, as in Tuesday’s reading.
vv: because you know that the testing of your faith produces endurance
Joy does not come from the trial itself but from what we know about it: God uses it to build our faith.
ask God, who gives to all generously and ungrudgingly, and it will be given you
Wisdom here is practical: how to live well, how to bear what we cannot change. God is a giver who does not reproach us for asking.
for the doubter, being double-minded and unstable in every way, must not expect to receive anything from the Lord
James is not speaking about the honest struggles of faith but about the person who asks while holding back from trusting God. Even a faltering faith can ask, and the Lord hears it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that prayer is a battle against ourselves and our own doubts, and that the answer to a lack of faith is to ask for it: “I believe; help my unbelief” (CCC 2728, citing Mark 9:24). The Church has always kept the call to endurance beside the call to joy: she honours the martyrs as those whose tested faith bore fruit in endurance to the end.

set: Mark places this story in two parts around the cleansing of the Temple (11:15–19), so that each explains the other. Jesus enters Jerusalem on Sunday, and this is Monday and Tuesday of that last week. Jesus is hungry, and he finds a fig tree “in leaf” with no fruit. Mark adds that it was not the season for figs.

In the prophets the fig tree and the vine are signs of Israel’s life with God, and a tree without fruit is a sign of judgement (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1). Most commentators therefore read the act as a parable in action: it warns about the Temple’s failure to be what God intended, “a house of prayer for all the nations” (11:17), aimed at its leadership and its use, not at the people of Israel. The Church teaches that the Jewish people remain beloved of God (Romans 11:28–29) and that Jesus’ Passion cannot be blamed on the Jews as a people (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4).
str: vv. 12–14: the hungry Jesus; the fig tree with leaves only; his word to it.
(vv. 15–19, not read today: the cleansing of the Temple.)
vv. 20–21: next morning: the tree withered to its roots; Peter remembers.
vv. 22–24: “Have faith in God”: the mountain; prayer with faith.
vv. 25–26: forgive when you stand praying.
kw: In v. 22 the Greek is echete pistin theou; Jesus literally says “have the faith of God”: some read it as faith in God, others as sharing God’s own faithfulness. Either way, it is trust that rests on who God is, not on our own power.
The word means to let go, to send away, and is the word for the forgiveness of debts in the Our Father. To forgive is to release what we hold against another before we come before God.
vv: he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.
A puzzle on the surface: why curse a tree for being out of season? Mark wants us to see that the story points beyond a tree. It is a sign of a time when God expected fruit and did not find it.

Jesus turns the disciples’ amazement into a lesson. The point is not power to destroy but trust in the one who can do what is humanly impossible. “This mountain” may mean the Temple Mount, close at hand; many think so.
Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone

Prayer and forgiveness go together. Faith does not stand apart from the heart that has been healed of its grudges. (Verse 26 is not in the NRSV text, since many ancient manuscripts omit it; it repeats Matthew 6:15, and it appears in the Malayalam Bible.)
ch: The Church hears in the withered fig tree both a warning and a call: God looks for fruit, and the fruit is love of God and neighbour. The Catechism teaches that Jesus asks for a faith that trusts (CCC 2609–2610), and that there can be no prayer to the Father without forgiving our brothers and sisters from the heart (CCC 2842–2845).

qa: Does Jesus promise that whatever we ask for in prayer will be given?

Jesus gives a strong promise, and the Church takes it seriously, but she reads it with the whole of Scripture. Jesus himself prayed in Gethsemane, “not what I want, but what you want” (Mark 14:36), and James adds that we can ask wrongly (4:3). Faith asks the Father with trust that he will give what is truly good, and the prayer of faith slowly conforms our wishes to his will (CCC 2737–2741).
rite: On 15 July the Syro-Malabar Church keeps the memorial of St Kuriakose (Cyriacus) and his mother St Julitta, martyrs. According to the traditional account, whose details are not all historically certain, Julitta, a Christian woman, fled with her young child during the persecution under Diocletian and was arrested at Tarsus. When the child confessed Christ before the governor, he was killed, and she was put to death after him. The Church remembers them as a pattern of faith in the family: a mother and her child who stayed faithful together. Daniel 3, with Azariah’s prayer in the furnace, and Matthew 10, “do not fear those who kill the body”, are the readings the Church gives for them.
study: James tells us to consider trials “nothing but joy”. What trial in my life might God use to build endurance, and what help should I ask?
Jesus joins prayer and forgiveness. Is there someone I need to forgive before I pray again, and how can I begin?
